title: How to perform Localization with Portable Object (PO) files in ASP.NET Core
description: Use Portable Object (PO) files for localization in ASP.NET Core.

data.text: Welcome to this comprehensive guide on **How to perform Localization with Portable Object (PO) files in ASP.NET Core**. Use Portable Object (PO) files for localization in ASP.NET Core. In today's rapidly evolving technology landscape, understanding this topic is crucial for any developer looking to build robust, scalable, and maintainable applications. This lesson will take you from fundamental concepts to advanced implementations, providing you with practical knowledge you can apply immediately. Whether you are a beginner taking your first steps or an experienced developer looking to deepen your expertise, this guide has something valuable for you. We will explore theoretical foundations, practical implementations, real-world scenarios, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end of this lesson, you will have a thorough understanding of How to perform Localization with Portable Object (PO) files in ASP.NET Core and be confident in applying it to your projects.
Some advantages of using PO files over resource files are:

items: PO files support pluralisation. I will explain it at the latter half of the tutorial.
PO files aren’t compiled like .resx files.
PO files work well with collaborative online editing tools.

data.text: Install the package ‘OrchardCore.Localization.Core’
First you need to install the package called OrchardCore.Localization.Core from NuGet.
Configuring the Website to use localization in Program class
Configuration involves adding the required services to the Program.cs. These are shown in highlighted color below:

data.text: In the above code I have specified that my website will support 3 cultures – ‘en-US’, ‘fr’ & ‘es’ i.e English US, French & Spanish, and it will be using PO files. The code services.AddPortableObjectLocalization() does this work for me.

Next, I specified the RequestLocalizationMiddleware to automatically set culture information for requests based on information provided by the client. This is done by adding app.UseRequestLocalization() middleare.
Creating PO files for French and Spanish cultures
As **Portable Object** files are merely text files which add from in Visual Studio. So create 2 text files on the root of your app, one for French and other for Spanish, and name then as:

items: fr.po
es.po

data.text: In the fr.po file add the following:

data.title: Code Example
data.content: Code example for How to perform Localization with Portable Object (PO) files in ASP.NET Core

data.text: msgid "Hello world!" msgstr "Bonjour le monde!"

data.title: Code Example
data.content: Code example for How to perform Localization with Portable Object (PO) files in ASP.NET Core

data.text: In the es.po file add the following:

data.title: Code Example
data.content: Code example for How to perform Localization with Portable Object (PO) files in ASP.NET Core

data.text: msgid "Hello world!" msgstr "¡Hola Mundo!"

data.title: Code Example
data.content: Code example for How to perform Localization with Portable Object (PO) files in ASP.NET Core

data.text: The PO files stores both the string to translate and the translated string. The syntax is:

items: msgid: The untranslated string.
msgstr: The translated string.

data.text: Here the PO files contains the translation of string called ’Hello world!’.
The ‘fr.po’ file is used if the requested culture is fr-FR, fr-CA and so on. Similarly the ‘es.po’ file is used if the requested culture is ‘es-MX’, ‘es-US’ and so on.
Reading translated values from PO files in Views
Whenever you have to localize your contents in the view then you have to make use of **IViewLocalizer** object. Simply inject it in your view like shown below:

data.title: Code Example
data.content: Code example for How to perform Localization with Portable Object (PO) files in ASP.NET Core

data.text: @using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Localization @inject IViewLocalizer Localizer

data.title: Code Example
data.content: Code example for How to perform Localization with Portable Object (PO) files in ASP.NET Core

data.text: Now you can simply display the translated string like:

data.title: Code Example
data.content: Code example for How to perform Localization with Portable Object (PO) files in ASP.NET Core

data.text: p@Localizer["Hello world!"]/p

data.title: Code Example
data.content: Code example for How to perform Localization with Portable Object (PO) files in ASP.NET Core

data.text: Testing

You can test the working by opening the view in the browser and adding the French culture in the URL as query string – ?culture=fr. You will see the translated string of ‘Hello world!’ in your browser.

You can also read the PO files content in the controller by using the IStringLocalizer object.

data.text: Using Pluralization in PO files

Not all languages follow the pluralisation format of English. So pluralisation feature comes into play. Here the cardinality of one is mapped to the first plural form. Any other cardinality is mapped to the second plural form. To include plural forms of a text use **msgid\_plural** entry in your PO file.
To see how it works, add the below texts in your ‘fr.po’ file.

data.title: Code Example
data.content: Code example for How to perform Localization with Portable Object (PO) files in ASP.NET Core
data.code:
msgid "There is one item."
msgid_plural "There are {0} items."
msgstr[1] "French text for first plural"
msgstr[2] "French text for second plural"

data.text: Next in your view add the below code to generated plural forms.

data.title: Code Example
data.content: Code example for How to perform Localization with Portable Object (PO) files in ASP.NET Core

data.text: p@Localizer.Plural(1, "There is one item.", "There are {0} items.")/p p@Localizer.Plural(2, "There is one item.", "There are {0} items.")/p

The msgctxt entry is used to limit entries in PO files to certain classes or views only.
For example, when I add the below shown texts in the ‘fr.po’ file, then only the ‘About’ view will show the translated word for ‘thanks’.
